presEras.label: The First Republic and the Estado Novo
presEras.blurb: Elected by parliament until 1918 and again after 1926, the presidency under Salazar was a formality with one exception: in 1958 General Delgado ran openly against the regime, was credited with 23% in a count nobody trusts, and was murdered by the secret police seven years later. Direct election was abolished immediately afterwards.

presEras.label: The presidency since the revolution
presEras.blurb: Directly elected again since 1976, on two rounds, with real powers of dissolution and veto that Portuguese presidents have used. Soares, Sampaio, Cavaco Silva and Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa each served the full two terms the constitution allows.

legEras.label: The First Republic
legEras.blurb: Sixteen years, forty-five governments and eight presidents, one of them assassinated. The republic that replaced the monarchy in 1910 never found a majority it could hold, and the elections of the period were run by whichever party controlled the ministry of the interior.

legEras.label: The Estado Novo
legEras.blurb: Salazar's New State held elections every four years for forty years and lost none of them. Opposition candidates were permitted to register and then denied the electoral rolls, access to the press and any prospect of an honest count; most withdrew before polling day. The National Union won every seat in every election listed here.

legEras.label: The Carnation Revolution
legEras.blurb: The captains' coup of April 1974 ended the dictatorship and the colonial wars together. The Constituent Assembly election of 1975, held on the revolution's first anniversary with a turnout of 91.7%, remains the highest participation in Portuguese history. What followed was a decade of minority governments, a hot summer of near civil war, and an IMF programme.

legEras.label: Cavaco and the two-party years
legEras.blurb: Cavaco Silva's absolute majorities in 1987 and 1991 ended the instability and set the pattern: the PSD and the PS alternating, each occasionally strong enough to govern alone, the Communists and the CDS reduced to flanks.

legEras.label: Troika and geringonça
legEras.blurb: The bailout of 2011 brought a right-wing majority and four years of austerity. In 2015 the right won the most votes and lost power anyway: the Socialists governed with the Communists and the Left Bloc supporting from outside, an arrangement the opposition named the geringonça, the contraption, and which lasted four years.

legEras.label: Three elections in three years
legEras.blurb: An absolute majority in 2022 that collapsed within two years, then elections in 2024 and 2025 with Chega rising at each one until it finished second. The Portuguese party system, stable for thirty years, has fragmented faster than any other in western Europe.
